The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Gangetic ailia (Ailia coila) was assessed from specimens collected during the pre-spawning season. Field surveys in the lower Ganges basin during the monsoon period yielded a mean gonadosomatic index of 8.78% [GSI = 8.78%] at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], consistent across all sampled gravid females. The incubation period for fertilised eggs under these same controlled thermal conditions was notably brief; hatching of the yolk-sac larvae commenced approximately 4 days [ab = approximately 4 days] after fertilisation, with complete eclosion of all viable embryos occurring within 24 hours of the first chorion rupture at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This rapid developmental phase is characteristic of teleost species that spawn in seasonally flooded habitats where transient nursery conditions demand swift progression through the earliest life stages to maximise larval survival.

At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the prolarvae of Ailia coila are minute, with a calculated wet weight at birth of 0.000029 grams [Wwb = 0.000029 grams], a mass derived from the mean egg diameter of approximately 0.38 millimeters observed in preserved ovarian samples. This remarkably small neonatal mass, among the lowest recorded for any freshwater catfish in the Indian subcontinent, imposes an extended period of vulnerability during the yolk-sac larval phase when individuals are entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves. The post-hatching developmental trajectory progresses through a distinct lecithotrophic stage lasting several days before the onset of exogenous feeding. The mouth opens and first exogenous feeding begins shortly after yolk-sac resorption, marking the critical trophic switch from maternally derived nutrients to active prey capture. Field observations of early-stage larvae in marginal floodplain habitats suggest that the availability of microzooplankton during this narrow window strongly influences recruitment success, as any delay in encountering suitable prey can lead to irreversible starvation before the point of no return is reached.

Sexual maturation in female Ailia coila occurs at a relatively small body size compared to other members of the Schilbidae family. Analysis of gonadal development across a size series of specimens collected from the Ganges and Brahmaputra river systems revealed that females attain puberty at a total length of 7.1 centimeters [Lp = 7.1 centimeters], a metric consistent across multiple sampling years and hydrological regimes. Coincident with this somatic milestone, the wet weight at puberty was recorded at 2.5 grams [Wwp = 2.5 grams], indicating that reproductive maturation is triggered not solely by chronological age but also by the attainment of a critical body mass threshold. This length-based maturation schedule likely reflects an adaptive strategy to balance the energetic demands of gamete production against the mortality risks associated with continued growth in a highly seasonal environment. Males of the species appear to mature at a slightly smaller size, though detailed histological data on testicular development remain limited. The relatively low body mass at puberty compared to ultimate body size suggests that A. coila adopts a life-history strategy prioritising early reproduction over extended somatic growth.

The ultimate total length attained by Ailia coila in natural populations was determined from extensive survey data and examination of museum collections spanning the species' known range. The maximum recorded total length reaches 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters], a value representing the upper asymptote of the growth curve for this species under favourable environmental conditions. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight, derived from length-weight regressions calibrated against field-caught specimens, reaches 211 grams [Wwi = 211 grams] for individuals approaching the asymptotic length. This relationship between body length and mass conforms closely to the general allometric pattern observed across freshwater siluriforms, though the species' slender, elongated body shape results in a relatively low mass per unit length compared to more deep-bodied catfishes, a morphological adaptation that reduces energetic costs during sustained swimming in turbid riverine environments. Longevity data from mark-recapture studies and otolith-based age estimation indicate that the maximum lifespan under natural conditions is 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], equivalent to approximately eight years, though most individuals in wild populations likely experience mortality considerably earlier due to predation pressure and habitat instability during monsoon floods.

Comparative analysis of life-history traits across the Schilbidae family highlights the relatively fast pace of life adopted by Ailia coila, particularly in its early developmental milestones and reproductive scheduling. The brief egg incubation period and small neonatal mass position this species toward the rapid end of the slow-fast continuum, a strategy well suited to ephemeral floodplain environments where growing seasons are short but resource abundance is seasonally high. In contrast, the maximum adult body mass of 211 grams [Wwi = 211 grams] and total body length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] are intermediate when compared to larger congeneric species such as Ailia punctata, which may exceed 45 centimeters in total length. The gonadosomatic index of 8.78% [GSI = 8.78%] was recorded in a species with a maximum lifespan of up to 2,920 days [am = up to 2,920 days] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Together, these demographic parameters describe a species that balances relatively early maturation at 7.1 centimeters [Lp = 7.1 centimeters] with sustained reproductive output over several years, a combination that appears well suited to the dynamic and unpredictable riverine ecosystems of the Indo-Gangetic plain, where seasonal flooding creates ephemeral but highly productive nursery habitats that favour rapid early development and modest adult body size.
